items.title: Market Highlights: November
items.excerpt: Despite the rain shower, it was a busy and very lovely market. Madre mia! As ever, our property master Lucy…
items.body_html:
Despite the rain shower, it was a busy and very lovely market.

Madre mia!

As ever, our property master Lucy Lee-Tirrell, dressed Buttercup to beautifully reflect the surprising Spanish cheeses from Brindisa that we tasted on Cheesewick HQ. Rain or shine, nothing dampens Buttercup’s bright spirits.

Ooh La La!

We are so pleased that the Bonnie Wheel has taken up the role of bringing excellent Scottish cheeses to the market and that Ooh La La, a soft Saint-Félicien-style, multiple award-winner from Highland Fine Cheeses is back on form and at the market. You can expect a silky, unctuous, lactic cow’s milk cheese with some luscious added cream… ooh la la indeed.

We have a winner! 

Alfie of European Fine Food held a competition to guess the weight of the Tête de Moine cheese and win both the cheese and a girolle and we got a winner who guessed the weight on the nose. Congratulations!

You’re my favourite! 

Cheesewick visitors were lucky enough to meet Jane Quicke, third-generation cheese maker from Quicke’s Cheddar. She was conducting some market research so anyone who tasted their cheddars at three different ages will have had a say in which cheese they focus on bringing to market. Stay tuned!!!

Next market

Next market is 20th December and you’ll be able to taste the cheese voted best in the world at the World Cheese Awards last week as it is stocked by The French Comté and it is a comté so please come and taste the best of the best.

items.title: Tasting Notes: November
items.excerpt: Delicious sheeps milk cheeses that prove Spain offers more than Manchego
items.body_html:
We had a wonderful tasting on Cheesewick HQ this month with Brindisa. We wanted to introduce market guests to unusual sheep’s milk cheeses from Spain, proving that there’s much more to Spanish cheese than Manchego.

In case you forgot and want to order some next time, here’s what we were tasting:

Zamorano Vicente Pastor, PDO
A traditional PDO Zamorano made from raw milk produced by the family’s own flock of indigenous Castellana sheep, grazing the plains of Zamora in northwestern Spain. Unlike many commercially finished cheeses, it retains its naturally moulded, unpainted rind. After approximately seven months of maturation, it develops a firm yet buttery texture, with a distinctive slight acidity and lingering cellar-aged notes that reflect its traditional production. Winner: Silver at the World Cheese Awards 2023

Torta de Barros
Made from raw sheep’s milk sourced from a single local farm in Extremadura, Torta de Barros uses cardoon flower (Cynara cardunculus) as its natural coagulant. This creates its characteristic almost-liquid, spoonable centre and a delicate, lingering bitterness that balances the richness of the sheep’s milk. Its distinctive character earned it the title of Best Spanish Cheese at the 2018 International Cheese Awards.Winner: Silver at the World Cheese Awards 2023.

“Pi” Mould-Ripened Raw Sheep’s Milk Cheese
Pi challenges conventional expectations of Manchega sheep’s milk cheeses. Produced at Finca Hualdo using milk from its own flock, it develops a mould-ripened rind and an unusually silky, semi-soft interior. Its flavour evolves from fresh, buttery and citrus notes towards earthy, herbal and nutty complexity near the rind. Awarded three stars at Great Taste in both 2025 and 2026, it demonstrates the remarkable versatility of raw Manchega sheep’s milk

When they sold out of the Pi, we added:

Villarejo Rosemary Cheese 

A Manchego-style cheese coated in Iberico pork fat and rosemary. The dairy is in Villarejo de Fuentes, in the heart of La Mancha and also produces authentic artisan Manchego cheese. They have 1,500 square meters of land over which the sheep graze freely ensuring superb milk. The cheese has a dense and lightly crunchy texture with buttery and herbal aromas.

Villarejo Rosemary Cheese

items.title: The French Comte’s winning bet: World’s Best Cheese comes to Chiswick Cheese Market this Sunday
items.excerpt: Like an excellent vintage of wine: when you know, you know
items.body_html:
f you haven’t already heard, a 24 month Comté PDO Fort des Rousses from Fromageries Arnaud was crowned the winner of the 2026 Guild of Fine Food’sorld Cheese Awards having beat out 5,330 entrants in Córdoba, Spain.

In a stunning boon for the Chiswick Cheese Market and for our customers, one of our traders actually stock this cheese and you can buy it tomorrow!

The French Comte, who specialise in French cheeses, are lucky enough to be stockists of this globally acclaimed cheese. However, this happy event doesn’t come about as haphazardly as you might imagine.

Started to showcase the produce from their native Franche-Comté region of eastern France, Roberto and Joel return each June or July to tour cheese caves in Jura. They taste cheese and choose the ones they would like to sell but the trick is, that was nearly two years ago. Like wine futures, they have to believe in the great blossoming of this cheese to come.

They visit many different producers and they have worked with Fromageries Arnaud in the past. They discussed the weather, the pasture, the herd and his hopes for the cheese with Jean-Charles Arnaud, a fourth generation cheesemaker, and they once they made their choice, the cheese was marked as theirs – for them and them alone – and because of that, FOR US!

Please come and grab your slice of world-wide winning Alpine cheese heaven – chosen when the hills were alive with flowers and music.

Roberto of The French Comte – he can pick a winner from a year off!

items.title: World Cheese Awards
items.excerpt: We are proud sponsors of the Young Cheesemonger of the Year Award
items.body_html:
Its award season in the world of artisan cheese but this week heralds the pinnacle of all the competitions – ‘The World Cheese Awards’. It’s a British run event (@guildoffinefood) but has captured the world of cheese and now has over 5,000 entries from over 40 countries. It is the only truly global cheese award ceremony.

Our very own Fran Warde will be flying the ‘Cheesewick’ flag for us and joining over 200 esteemed International Judges gathering, with the cheeses, in Cordoba and on Thursday the Champion will be crowned.

Alongside this mind-boggling amount of cheese sits a newer but no less important competition to find the ‘Young Cheesemonger of the Year’. Run by @acedemyofcheese, we are the main sponsors of this competition with Peters Yard. The large field of entrants from all over the world has been reduced to 8 finalists showing off their skills and knowledge as fledgling cheese mongers. With several challenges in front of an audience and a quick fire round of cheese knowledge, the finalists will need nerves of steel while they show off their skills – may the best cheesemonger win!

You can follow the action live at World Cheese Awards TV

World Cheese Awards

and follow updates @academyofcheese

Stay tuned for highlights from Fran upon her return from Cordoba!

items.title: Queen Mary returns to ‘Cheesewick’
items.excerpt: Free tasting: sample three Quicke’s cheddars to find your favourite
items.body_html:
Mary Quicke has been making Cheddar on their family farm in Devon for decades; she is a founder of The Academy of Cheese and has been at the forefront of the renaissance of the British Artisan cheese industry since the 70s. She is in a word, most definitely ‘The Queen’ of cheese making in the UK.

When Mary wanted to find out which age of their cheddar was the most loved, we were thrilled when she thought the best place to ask that question was here at ‘Cheesewick’. So, she is asking you to blind taste three ages of her cheddar with her and then you have the chance to buy your favourite from Cheeswick’s own King of cheddar – Roi. Don’t miss this rare opportunity to meet one of the most experienced, most informative and loveliest cheesemakers in the industry. Look out for Roi’s giant cheddar stack and you will find Mary next door waiting to say hello.

Roi’s rich stack of cheese

items.title: Cheddar Cheese, Chilli and Courgette bundles
items.excerpt: Cheddar Cheese, Chilli and Courgette bundles by Fran Warde Elevate the simple courgette to these delicious vegetable addition to any…
items.body_html:
Cheddar Cheese, Chilli and Courgette bundles

by Fran Warde

Elevate the simple courgette to these delicious vegetable addition to any meal, you can easily change the cheese to your favourite but I like making them with a classic West Country Cheddar.

makes 6

preparation 25 minutes

cooking 45 minutes

4 / 5 medium courgettes

150g west country cheddar, grated

chilli flakes

freshly ground black pepper

Heat the oven to 200C

Using a vegetable peeler, draw ribbons off the length of the courgettes.

Arrange a layer, slightly overlapping the edges and ends of the courgette ribbons, making a sheet of approx 12cm high 48cm length.

Sprinkle with 1 6th of the grated cheese, chilli flakes and pepper.

Carefully fold and roll the courgette sheet from one end to the other and place end up in a silicone muffin tray or a lightly oiled muffin tin and gently push the top down with the palm of your hand. This helps make it more compact.

Repeat until all 6 are prepared top with a little extra cheese and place in the oven to cook.

Reduce the temperature after 25 minutes to 180C they should be golden and bubbling. Cook for a further 20 mins.

Serve and enjoy on their own or as part of a meal.

items.title: Lucy’s November 2026 Cheese of the Month: Tête de Moine
items.excerpt: A punchy Alpine cheese served up as a bouquet of flowers
items.body_html:
Tête de Moine is a cylindrical, washed, semi-soft, raw cow milk cheese weighing just under a kilo. It has a fine-grained texture that melts in the mouth, and the milk is from the lush spring pastures of the mountains of the Bernese-Jura region which gives it a distinctive Alpine  flavour. It is matured for a minimum of 10 weeks on pine boards in one of only 8 registered Tête de Moine dairies.

First made by the monks who arrived in the 12th century ‘Tête de Moine’ means ‘Monk’s head’ and there are many historical references to the monks paying for the use of land and buildings with their cheese. Its name may simply have been a ‘head count’ and reference for amount paid rather than a derisory term referring to its likeness to a monk’s shaved head!

Most commonly we see this cheese being sold in rosettes or ‘flowers’ made by shredding the cheese very thinly with a ‘Girolle’ (a sharp blade that rotates and shaves very thin slices in a circular motion resulting in flower-like bundles). In fact, this machine was not invented until 1981 so you most certainly do not need one of these to enjoy this cheese.  Tête de Moine won its first cheese medals at the Paris World Exhibition as early 1856 – so it has been enjoyed for far longer than the Girolle has been around!

So, what does it taste like? It is a firm dense texture like its Alpine counterparts but for me it has a deeper richer flavour even at 2 ½ months – its less fruity and sweeter, yeastier and more savoury than young Comté or a June made Beaufort and the washed rind is most definitely more pungent on the nose. Because this has both a deep texture and flavour (which gets deeper and richer as it matures) I enjoy a crisp, minerally white wine with it,  but if I have it on a cheeseboard after a meal,  I would equally enjoy it with a Riesling or if I wanted red, a Chianti with its cherry notes.

This is, however, one of my favourite cooking cheeses – it’s intense savouriness adds real umami to almost any dish and it pairs really well with autumn flavours – I add it to mushroom risotto rather than parmesan – try grating it, stirring it with a little mascarpone to make a thick paste to top crusty bread and make a quite incredible cheese on toast!  I also love to use the shredded ‘flowers’ piled high to top bruschetta. This is much smaller in size than its Alpine cousins but what it does not have in size, it makes up for in flavour as it packs a powerful, pungent punch on the palate. Alpine cheese lovers – you will not be disappointed!

Alfie @europeanfinecheese stall will be selling the cheese cut or shaving its distinctive flowers using a traditional girolle machine. Don’t miss their competition this month to win your very own Girolle machine.

items.title: Grantee Update: Film Premiere!
items.excerpt: We said it was coming, and now it’s here: premiere! As we’ve happily reported previously, our 2025 Chiswick Cheese Market…
items.body_html:
We said it was coming, and now it’s here: premiere!

As we’ve happily reported previously, our 2025 Chiswick Cheese Market Grantee, Jake Goldstein, has thrown himself into cheesemaking with an inspiring – and award-winning – passion. When Sam Brice, a marketing professional who tells the stories of independent makers, ran across Jake, it was a natural fit. RAW: The Story of a Small Cheese follows Jake’s journey from running cocktail bars in Brighton to making his own cheese on the Welbeck Estate.

The Chiswick Cheese market was pleased to also help sponsor the making of this films and it includes cameos from Chiswick Cheese Market members Lucy Cufflin and Fran Warde, as well as Tracey Colley of the Academy of Cheese, our co-sponsors of the grant programme.

We are organizing a viewing of the film in early 2027 so please stay tuned. 

RAW: The Story of a Small Cheese will be released online on Wednesday 4 November. See the trailer below.

items.title: Redlap and Fresh Chive Scones
items.excerpt: Delicious savoury scones which are perfect for this time of the year as the weather gets chilly. The Redlap…
items.body_html:
Delicious savoury scones which are perfect for this time of the year as the weather gets chilly. The Redlap hard goats cheese adds a delicious umami flavour, enjoy while warm with butter.

Oven temp 210C, Cooking time 10 mins, Prep time 20 mins

Makes 10 using and 8cm cookie cutter

Ingrediants

150g Redlap cheese

20g Parmesan, grated

250g self raising flour

10g baking powder

1 teaspoon bicarbonate of soda

100g butter, diced

1/2 teaspoon salt

Handful fresh chives, chopped

100g milk

60g plain yoghurt

1 egg

1. Cover a baking sheet with a layer of baking parchment.

2. Grate the Redlap cheese finely onto a plate, also grate the Parmesan add to the plate, place in the freezer while making the dough. This helps the to be looser and not stick together when added to the dough.

3. Put the flour, baking powder, bicarbonate of soda, salt and butter into a mixing bowl.

4. Using your hands rub the butter and flour mix together running your thumbs over your fingers until the mix is evenly blended and resembles coarse breadcrumbs. Shake the mixing bowl while blending and the larger lumps will come to the top.

5. Add the chives and chilled grated cheeses and mix well with your hands until evenly distributed.

6. In another bowl mix the milk, yoghurt, and egg with a fork, add to the dry mix and using the fork bring the mix together, until evenly blended. It will be a very wet soft dough.

7. Flour the work top well and turn out the wet dough onto the surface, dust with a little more flour and then either using a rolling pin or your hands and a very light and quick touch shape into a 2-3cm thick sheet.

8. Dip the cutter base in flour and then cut out the scones and place them into the baking sheet. Reform left over dough and cut out more.

9. Brush the tops of the scones with milk and bake in the oven for 10 minutes.

8. Dip the cutter base in flour and then cut out the scones and place them into the baking sheet. Reform left over dough and cut out more.

9. Brush the tops of the scones with milk and bake in the oven for 10 minutes.

items.title: Lucy’s October 2026 Cheese of the Month: Redlap
items.excerpt: A goats cheese and an Alpine cheese – yes, it can be both!
items.body_html:
Martin and Helen Boyd bought the farm in 2024 just near Dartmouth after years working in Finance at home and abroad.

It’s a beautiful slice of paradise – fields looking out to sea near Dartmouth. Martin had a dream to create a British version of Comté, his favourite cheese. Having planned to rear cows he was informed in no uncertain terms by new neighbours that the land had been home to goats since the Doomsday book and it was most certainly goat country not cow pasture. Not to be daunted Martin duly bought goats and set about experimenting to create a Goat version of an Alpine cheese.

A little bit of cheese knowledge for you here – Comté is a hard cheese and belongs to a set of cheeses known as ‘cooked pressed cheeses’. This means once the curd and whey are separated, the whey remains around the curd and is heated from its ‘cheese make temperature’ of about 32C to 55C. It is this heating that drives off moisture, gives Alpines their tight, slightly chewy texture and helps them to be fabulous melters. It also kills some bacteria and activates other cultures that give that traditional nutty Alpine flavour. Goats’ milk will not tolerate these temperatures, so it was Martin’s chemistry background that helped him create a recipe using some Alpine starter cultures and raise the temperature it their absolute limit (the actual temp remains a secret) and create what is most definitely a triumph of a cheese – ‘Redlap’. The pastures have been planted adding wildflowers and clover and the goats graze here happily looking out over Redlap Bay. One year after creating this extraordinary cheese Martin and Helen won the Best New British Cheese at The People’s Choice 2025. Cheesewick are very happy sponsors of this important award where only public votes count. I had the opportunity to champion this cheese on the night of the final and lead everyone through the tasting so, in order to do that I visited Helen and Martin and experienced the joy, love and passion that goes into this cheese. They truly believe that happy goats will make wonderful cheese and I for one totally agree with them and boy are their goats a happy crowd. It is the Final again of this fantastic competition and we are happy to host all four 2026 finalists on HQ this month so I thought this was a perfect opportunity to properly introduce you to Redlap, the 2025 winner.

So, lets talk about the cheese……

It’s a large wheel with a delightful orangey brown washed rind. Its texture is firm but giving when you cut into it allowing the cheese to offer a wonderful ‘chew’ in the mouth. It’s so much sweeter than you would imagine a goat cheese – by using Alpine starter cultures the cheese as a savoury nuttiness reminiscent of its cow milk mountain cousins but with a tang at the end that just lets you know this cheese is not a standard Alpine. The combination for me is quite magical.

It’s a great cheeseboard cheese and holds it head high amongst blues and softer cheeses. It pairs beautifully with apples or apple chutney, and its slight tang allows it to complement sweeter dried fruits perfectly. Although it is not quite the melter that we expect from an Alpine it made one of the best toasties I have ever had, adding a few walnuts in between the bread.

This is a gateway goats’ cheese – so if you don’t think you like goat, I urge you to try this.

I drank a rather big Chardonnay with it, but I think it also sits well with an IPA.

I made delectable cheese scones with it and some utterly mouthwatering Redlap and fresh chive savoury biscuits for aperitifs. This is an ‘all-rounder’. Eat it on its own, cook with it, hero it on a cheeseboard – I assure you this cheese will not disappoint.

Available from Justin on @no2poundst this month.

items.title: Grantee Update: Jake Goldstein’s winning streak
items.excerpt: A Forkful (or two) of Nottingham
items.body_html:
Jake Goldstein of Primrose Creamery, one of our 2025 Chiswick Cheese Market Cheesemaker Grant recipients, has set the Nottinghamshire cheese world rolling.

Founded in October of 2025 on the Welbeck Estate in Nottingham, Jake’s Primrose Creamery is dedicated to making great cheese, rooted in the land. The milk is delivered warm from the cows and each cheese is named after local person associated with cheese.

Lindley is a soft, raw cow’s milk cheese enriched with Jersey cream named after Elizabeth Lindley who was an unassuming but essential dairymaid on the Welbeck Estate.

Eggleston, another raw milk cheese, is small and soft with a delicate, orange rind and a gently ripening centre. Although William Eggleston took no part in the violence of the 1766 Cheese Riot, he was a Nottinghamshire farmer who was only trying to protect his produce but was killed nonetheless.

Jake’s desire to get his cheeses noticed led him to enter the British and Irish Cheese Awards where he won silver for Lindley and bronze for Eggleston. Next came the Artisan Cheese Awards where Primrose Creamery won five golds, four silvers and three bronzes as well as young cheesemaker of the year for Jake.

In the September 2026 Great Taste Awards, both cheeses were awarded three stars each and then went on to win an outstanding two Golden Forks. The Great Taste Golden Fork for England went to Eggleston and the Golden Fork for Outstanding Bursary Winner was handed to Lindley.

The Chisweek Cheese Market was also approached by Sam Brice about supporting his short documentary film about Jake’s cheese journey. We are eagerly anticipating the release of the film and more progress from the seemingly unstoppable Primrose Creamery.

The grant provides instruction from The Academy of Cheese and Jake is embarking on Level Three with a view to Master of Cheese accreditation.

items.title: Fine Cheesemakers of Scotland shine at the September market
items.excerpt: Bringing Highland ‘Reelness’ to Cheesewick
items.body_html:
The Chiswick Cheese Market is the monthly home to over 250 different artisan cheeses from around the world and while many are from within the UK, we do not feature as many Scottish cheeses as we would like. In September we enlisted the help of Morgane Lambert and Emma Johnson from Fine Cheese Makers of Scotland to reel in some Scottish artisan cheesemakers and showcase the Flower of Scotland’s cheeses as it were.

HQ – the monthly market headquarters of all things cheesy – was host to two Scottish producers.

Rory Stone of Highland Fine Cheeses, a man self-professed to be obsessed with ‘smelly little things’ brought his award-winning and fragrant Minger, Morangie Brie and Blue Murder all made at their farm in Tain from milk from The Black Isle.

The Stewart family have farmed in Falside in Fife since the 1930’s. Jane Stewart brought the farm’s St. Andrews Cheese raw milk Anster as well as their Whiskey Barrel Smoked St. Andrew cheddar.

Faye, of Big Wheel cheese who specialise in cheeses from all over the British Isles, was delighted to add an extra stall bedecked with Saltires and laden with Scottish cheeses. By midday all the Minger was gone.

Augmenting the Scottish flare was the extraordinary bagpiping talent, Duncan Grant a master of Great Highland Bagpipe. He serenaded a tartaned Buttercup and marched the length and breadth of the market, certainly a man at the height of his ‘skirl’ power.

Kilts a kimbo, tam o’shanters a plenty, a slew of Saltires, scads of bagpipe skirls – it was a REELY good time!

items.title: Lucy’s September 2026 Cheese of the Month: Minger
items.excerpt: A fragrance from the Highlands
items.body_html:
Made by Highland Fine Cheeses
Milk: Cow

Minger has long been a favourite of mine so I am thrilled that it will be found at Cheesewick this month and I can at last really shout about it.

Made by the Stone family in the Highlands it is a soft pungent, washed-rind cows’ milk cheese. It has a sticky bright orange rind coloured with natural annatto and is named after the Scottish slang word for something foul-smelling (ming!).

Rory who will attend the September market, has been known to describe the smell as like that of an old welly boot, but don’t let that put you off – despite its ‘barnyard’ nose the inside is buttery, smooth and as it ripens gloriously gooey. It tastes distinctively ‘savoury’ and mildly nutty. Its bark is much worse than its bite!

I adore it on any cheeseboard, but I do have a secret vice with this cheese – I absolutely love it on slightly burnt sourdough toast topped with a thick layer of bitter marmalade – for me an almost unparalleled weekend indulgence! My culinary quirks aside, this cheese pairs very well with ripe fruits and oatcakes. For whisky drinkers this is a fabulous combo but if you want to enjoy this cheese as a lighter snack then I love it with a crisp white wine as I like the juxtaposition of the tartness of the wine and the creamy richness of the cheese. A good strong ale will sit happily alongside, and I urge you to taste this cheese this Sunday. Overcome its smell and you will discover a cheese which undoubtably become a firm favourite.

items.title: Meet the 2026 Chiswick Cheese Market Cheesemaker Grantees!
items.excerpt: Introducing the some of the UK’s promising new cheesemakers
items.body_html:
One of our driving missions is to help preserve, support and promote artisan cheese-making in the UK so a highlight in the year is when we select, in collaboration with the Academy of Cheese, the new candidates who will receive the Chiswick Cheese Market Cheesemaker Grant. We had a record number of applications this year which made for exciting and difficult decisions but we are delighted to introduce the three 2026 recipients.

When Ethan Parry started Usk Valley Dairy with his parents in 2025, the ambition was clear: to make distinctive, small-batch cheeses using locally sourced milk in the Usk Valley.

Today, Ethan is running a purpose-built micro-dairy in South Wales, producing Gouda-style and Brie-style cheeses for farm shops, delis and food events.

Having been awarded one of this year’s three Chiswick Cheese Market Cheesemakers’ Grants, Ethan now has the opportunity to build on everything he has learned so far and develop the deeper technical understanding needed to consistently produce exceptional cheese.

“Everything so far has been very hands-on and largely self-taught,” Ethan explains. “That’s been great to a point, but now I want to understand more about the cheese we’re making.”

Please read the full article detailing Ethan’s cheese-making development on the Academy of Cheese’s website, here.

For Richard Inman, cheesemaking is the culmination of a long-standing fascination with how food is made.

His journey began at home, making cheese for friends and family. What started as an experiment gradually became something more serious, and in 2024 he founded the Buckinghamshire Cheese Company with the ambition of creating a truly local artisan cheese.

Now, after 18 months spent securing regulatory approvals, building food safety systems and fitting out his dairy, Richard is ready to bring his first cheese to market.

“The grant will help me close the gap between a cheese that is promising and a cheese that is consistently good,” he says. “And that is the difference that matters most right now.”

Read more about Richard’s extraordinary story and his promising blue cheese here.

Harriet McPhee has spent the past six years producing milk for artisan cheesemakers. Now, with a growing flock of dairy sheep, a herd of goats and an ambitious plan for her own cheesemaking enterprise, she is taking the next step: from supplying cheesemakers to becoming one herself.

Harriet’s journey into small-scale dairy farming began in March 2020 with just two goats. Six years later, she and her husband Chris are milking goats and sheep in Cumbria, supplying artisan cheesemakers across Cumbria and Yorkshire.

But the changing landscape of the artisan cheese industry has prompted Harriet to rethink the future of the business.

“Quite a lot of our markets have gone in the last year, or people have retired,” she explains. “We thought, well, we’ve got the milk, so let’s add value to it ourselves.”

That decision has led Harriet to apply for, and be awarded, a Chiswick Cheese Market Cheesemakers Grant, giving her the opportunity to develop the technical cheesemaking skills she needs to turn her milk into cheese.

Find out more about Harriet’s evolution as a farmer and cheese-maker here.

items.title: Lucy’s August 2026 Cheese of the Month: Robiola ‘tre latti’
items.excerpt: A delicate blend of three different milks: a winning trifecta!
items.body_html:
Medhi, on Gastronomica Market stall, brings this cheese every month to Cheesewick. It’s not seasonal in the fact that it is only made at certain times of the year, it is made all year round, but what makes this cheese exceptional at this time of the year is beautifully fragrant summer milks (this cheese is only 15 days old when we see it at the market).

Eligio Castagna started making cheeses from ancient recipes in the Piedmont region of Italy over 60 years ago and now the dairy, run by his son, Guiseppe continues to make cheeses using only the best local milk from animals reared in unspoilt valleys and mountains in the Piedmont, using methods that take time and old-fashioned hands-on skills.

Robiola cheese is a style that has many variants depending on the milk used (can be cow, sheep, goat or a combination of any of those three) and very different depending on its age. A small round cheese with a delicate wriggly rind. It has a dense buttery texture when it is fresh with a citrus milky flavour but as it ages it becomes oozy and unctuous with more robust mushroomy, nutty farmyard flavours.

I adore goat and sheep cheeses, but I know this is not everyone’s cup of tea. This unique cheese made from a combination of cow, goat and sheep milks, seems to me to answer my desire for the distinct flavours I love, whilst blending them with the full fat, rich cows’ milk, making it a much easier cheese for those who don’t think they like the taste of goat milk. You simply must have a go, even if you are not a goats’ cheese lover!

At this time of year, the cheeses start to get richer as the milking season progresses (milk can be richer towards the end of the milking season as babies start to eat the grass and come to Mum for extra nourishment rather than an entire meal – less volume more intense goodness). It is this richness combined with the outdoor pastures that make this cheese so special now. The second reason is that I think these soft lactic set cheeses are a joy in this hot weather. Soft and spreadable on crackers or even with raw vegetables they can be part of the ultimate ‘picky-bits’ platter. I always buy two of these and start one almost as soon as we’ve packed the market away, but I keep one carefully stored in my wine fridge (about 9C) for a couple of weeks until it starts to ripen and I can feel it oozing inside its wrapper. Then I open a bottle of fizz. I simply adore the combination of this indulgent, creamy, rich cheese mixed with the bubbles on my tongue. Sometimes pairing is not just about the flavour – sometimes it is about the satisfaction of the texture combination created and this is one I thoroughly recommend.

Made by The Castagna Dairy, Piedmont, Italy
Milk: Three types – cow, sheep and goats

items.excerpt: In these hot summer days this is a refreshing and light salad that is also quick to make. Classically made…
items.body_html:
In these hot summer days this is a refreshing and light salad that is also quick to make. Classically made with feta but I love the rich buttery, tangy flavours that the Manchego adds you can also try goats cheese, Halloumi Mozzarella or Pecorino.

Perfect as a light lunch salad but also goes very well with grilled white fish, roast chicken or steaks.

At the market the girls on Brindisa and Tom of Finer Things deli have a great selection of Manchego’s.

items.title: Lucy’s June 2026 Cheese of the Month: Pevensey Blue
items.excerpt: A heavenly, award-winning blue from Sussex – it’s on the level!!
items.body_html:
If you know me, then it will be no surprise to see Pevensey Blue pop up here as my cheese of the month at some point – it is always in my top 5 cheeses every single time I revise that list. It is made in East Sussex by Martin and Hazel Tkalez, using organic milk from the next-door Court Lodge Farm, in a dairy built on Hazel’s family beef farm.

After 15 years working in the cheese business, first at Neal’s Yard Dairy and then a year at Trethowan Brothers, Martin along with his wife Hazel took the plunge and made their dream a reality. They didn’t feel they could compete with Stilton in the nation’s hearts, so they based their recipe on Gorgonzola.

This is a wonderful cheese – I must tell you that for me it does not win prizes for looks – but never judge a book by its cover as its taste and texture are a remarkable combo. Its blue veining is not abundant but so well balanced across the flavour of the cheese as a whole. On cutting the cheese it yields to the knife in a soft fudgy way giving you just a little glimpse of the joy of the dreamy mouthfeel to come. Its flavour is big but not frightening in a Roquefort way. It is indulgent in a way clotted cream is more indulgent than its non-clotted sister. Its smooth but not bland, salted perfectly and I think that they have achieved their goal in wanting to create a cheese that is not too blue, not too salty but ridiculously moreish. Nutty, creamy, piquant and just enough farmyard notes to know you are eating a true Artisan cheese. Awarded Supreme Champion at The Artisan Cheese Awards in 2022, literally a few months after the first batches were released for sale.

So why now? The cheese we are enjoying now is made of milk from the cows that have been put out in the fields in the spring, and I believe that this liberation and abundance of fresh spring grasses and flowers do make a real difference to the milk. The balance of proteins and butterfat in the milk at that time reflect this. Theoretically this should allow a greater number of those delicious blue veins and allow the paste to mature to that adorable fudge-like texture. These are minor changes and to be honest with you by concentrating hard for several years on perfecting one cheese (rather than being distracted by inventing several new cheeses at once) Martin and Hazel have achieved a consistency in Pevensey Blue that is rare to find in the world of artisan cheese making.

I love it with fresh pears but if you match it with something sweet like sticky port-soaked raisins you create an indulgent pudding like sensation which lifts this cheese to another level. I like it with sourdough crackers or something crunchy because it works well with the fondant texture of the cheese.

Fay @bigwheelcheese was one of the first people to sell this cheese and champions it wherever she is standing market. She will have it, as usual, this month on her stall at Cheesewick and I recommend it thoroughly to blue cheese and non-blue-cheese lovers alike. I know after tasting it I will not be the only one who has this on their list of top 5 cheeses – enjoy!

items.title: Lucy’s July 2026 Cheese of the Month: Eggleston Reserve
items.excerpt: Proud Market Moment: Chiswick Cheesemaker Grantee makes a delicious award-winning cheese!
items.body_html:
‘Eggleston’ made by Jake Goldstein, recently crowned ‘Young Cheesemaker of the Year’ at the 2026 Artisan Cheese awards, is my cheese of the month.

Jake spent over a decade in food and drink owning a cocktail bar and running hospitality experiences. Covid proved to be a turning point and he decided to follow a career in cheese, training with Neal’s Yard Creamery. Jake applied for our New Cheesemakers Grant in 2025 after a long spell making cheese with one of our other grantees, Dean at Monkland Cheese. Jake has established ‘The Primrose Creamery’ within the buildings of The School of Artisan food at Welbeck. This is not Jake’s first cheese – ‘Lindley’ has won awards nationwide and we can buy it regularly at the market from Justin at No. 2 Pound St.

Eggleston is a small round raw cow’s milk cheese washed with annatto to give it a distinctive thin orange slightly pungent orange rind. When it is young it is firm and fresh, with clean bright flavours of lemon zest and cultured cream. As it matures (and this, for me, is where it becomes a truly special cheese) the edges soften to a fudgy consistency bringing flavours of ripe pear, sweet butter and a hint of farmyard straw that reminds me I am eating a truly artisan made cheese. The texture is velvety and that tells me that this cheese is made with love, and the curd has been treated gently and with respect all the way along its journey from the richest, locally sourced milk to this extraordinary little cheese packed with flavour.

The cheese is named after William Eggleston who lost his life in the 1766 Nottingham Cheese Riot – not because he was rioting but because he was trying to protect his cheeses. Jake reflects this protective nature about making cheese and he says “We make cheese led by flavour: bright, rich, deep and shifting with time. Each one helps you reconnect with the land, carrying stories of people and place to share at your table.” Hats off to you Jake, this cheese is a triumph, and at Chiswick Cheese Market we are proud to have played a very small part along your cheese journey.

If that does not sound exciting enough Justin will be bringing all of Jake’s stock of ‘Eggleston Reserve’. This is a carefully matured version of the Eggleston with its own tasting notes. This is a rare cheese indeed and if you are keen to get your hands on this then you’ll need to be early to the market!

What do I pair my Eggleston with? Well, when it is young and firm, I love it in a crisp lettuce salad washed down with a light white wine, but as it matures I enjoy it with a cracker, sweet pears and either a Riesling or even a fruity cider. Come along and see what you think.

items.title: The people spoke and their answer was Cheesewick!
items.excerpt: The Affineur of the Year Awards’ People’s Choice Award goes to Chiswick Cheese Market!
items.body_html:
When we started the Chiswick Cheese Market in 2021, we set out to support cheese makers and cheese mongers but we had no idea what an adventure it would turn out to be. The market was founded and is run by a group of impassioned volunteers who donate their time and the proceeds of the market to charity. To date we have given £75,000 to support various causes.

Our championing of artisan cheese makers quickly garnered the attention of the Academy of Cheese, the UK’s professional accreditation association who are dedicated to fostering cheese knowledge, cheese education and careers in cheese.

We have collaborated with the Academy to offer the Chiswick Cheese Market Grant to help educate, mentor and promote the blossoming of artisan cheesemaking throughout the United Kingdom. To date, we have given 12 grants and about to offer 3 more for 2026.

One of the most important events in the UK artisan cheese-making calendar is the Academy of Cheese’s Affineur of the Year Awards. An affineur is akin to a ‘cheese-whisperer,’ an expert in the art of maturing and ageing cheese, otherwise known as affinage. Great affinage is equal parts alchemy, understanding and collaboration between the cheesemaker and cheesemonger and the elements.

A highly competitive contest, the Affineur of the Year joins the forces of the educators, cheesemakers and the affineur and we have been proud sponsors of the Hard Cheese category for three years. The entrants are attempting to push boundaries with the cheeses, explore new techniques and showcase their cheese and maturing artistry and skill. Historically, several new cheeses have come out of the competition.

How it works: There are five categories of cheese in the competition. Hard Cheese, Soft Cheese, a Washed Rind cheese, a Crumbly cheese and a Blue cheese. Each participant receives the same cheese made from the same herd, the same batch of milk and made on the same day. They then have the remaining amount of time to implement their ageing and maturing plan. The judges are looking for not only great tasting cheese, but that the method of maturing chosen displays both knowledge and the skill to achieve that outcome.

For the second year in a row, the Chiswick Cheese Market waded into the competition as competitors, not just sponsors. We chose the Cropwell Bishop Stilton – possibly one of the greatest and grandest of British cheeses to see what we could achieve.

Because virtually all cheese is made from the same four ingredients (milk, starter cultures – beneficial bacteria, rennet and salt) how, when and at what temperature and to what degree these ingredients are added define the cheese. To make Stilton, pasteurised cow’s milk is inoculated with starter cultures, rennet and Penicillium roqueforti at 32C. The curds are drained of the whey, salted and chopped by hand and then placed into tall cylindrical hoops. The curds are drained and compacted by gravity and not pressed which gives Stilton its slightly crumbly texture.

The curds have to develop before any oxygen is introduced (oxygen is what activates the Penicillium roqueforti and produces the blue-mould veining), so the sides of the cheeses are smoothed by hand to seal out any oxygen. The cheeses are kept in humidity-controlled refrigerated room for 10 days at 10-12C and 85% humidity for 3-4 weeks. They are turned daily for the first 10 days to ensure even moisture throughout the cheese.  Only after the cheese is fully-formed is the cheese mechanically rodded to introduce oxygen and create the beautiful, distinctive blue-veining. The Stilton is aged for another 8-10 weeks in a temperature and humidity controlled environment to encourage the blue-veining throughout the cheese and develop the rind.

We had our Stilton ‘Gotcha Day’ when she – yes, she was a she and she was our Cheese Baby – was only ten days old and weighed eight kilos!

Our market has developed into a beautiful collaboration with Chiswick and its community and our traders and the wider cheese world. We wanted to celebrate that cooperation in our cheese. Our idea for our Cheese Baby was to invite her down from Nottingham (where she was born) for a pint and a cheeky fag at the George IV on Chiswick High Road.

We turned and washed the 8k wheel of cheese in local Fullers’ Vintage Ale (8% alc) provided by the George IV pub for the first eleven days keeping the humidity high to encourage mould growth. Stilton is not a washed rind cheese but we wanted to see how the ale would influence the flavour. Then we pierced her by hand – it was painful for us but it was for a good cause: the blue veins. After we had her for four weeks, we escorted her to London Smoke & Cure who are one of the fantastic traders at our market and are master smokers. They smoked her whole for four days (Stilton is regularly smoked but after it has been fully matured and then, only in smaller pieces, not whole) before she came home to Chiswick where we kept a watchful eye on the temperature and humidity. What we lacked in depth and breadth of knowledge and experience, we more than made up for with tender, loving daily care from a team six doting Cheese Mamas. It takes a village to raise a cheese.

The Affineur of the Year Awards took place at Christchurch Spitalfields this year and is open to the public. Along with the prizes for best cheese which is judged on technical skill, innovation and planned outcomes, there is also the People’s Choice for each cheese. Everyone present votes for the People’s Choice, the judges, the cheesemakers, the cheesemongers and the public. It is awarded to the cheese people most liked to eat, that tastes the very best.

We were thrilled and astonished to see how much of the glorious blue veining we had achieved. The ale lent a Marmite-y taste which complimented and enhanced the blue. The paste was creamy and the smoking lent a ‘bacon and Stilton toasty’ taste. Hugely enjoyable and very satisfying to us, nascent affineurs as we are.

Dear reader: we won the People’s Choice Award for our Cheese Baby! Oh, Cheese Baby, we’ll eat you up, we love you so!

items.title: Seasonal Sensation: Wild Garlic in May
items.excerpt: Hurray, hurray! The first of May! It’s not just the season for hedgerow tupping, it’s also Wild Garlic time!
items.body_html:
IT’S MAY: GO WILD… GARLIC!

The first of May is celebrated and heralded in a number of ways: Hurray, hurray! The first of May! Hedgerow tupping begins today! It is also wild garlic season so do try Yarg wrapped in wild garlic from Fay at Big Wheel Cheese – less than 6 weeks old this classic lactic cheese from Cornwall is wrapped very young in local wild garlic leaves giving it a hint of garlic flavour.

Alfie at European Fine Cheese is bringing Bärlauchkäse a Swiss Alpine cheese with wild garlic and fresh local herbs mixed with the milk – think classic Alpine texture and flavour tinged with the aroma and taste of those Alpine meadows.

Patrick at Curd & Cure is bringing a wonderful Cornish Brie layered with wild garlic which marries the creaminess of the Brie paste and the fresh herbiness of the wild garlic perfectly.

Jenny from Nut Knowle Farm will be bringing fresh goat cheese wrapped in wild garlic leaves which are very pretty little parcels tied up with string!

It’s not just cheese as the team at The Olive Bar are bringing wild garlic and pork saucisson with them this month – we can’t wait to try it!

items.title: Lucy’s May 2026 Cheese of the Month: Pyghtle
items.excerpt: Chiswick Cheese Market Cheesemaker grantee, Emily Tydeman, is making a delicious and unusual lactic set sheep milk log
items.body_html:
We all tried this cheese last September at the market when Emily Tydeman sent us some to try at our ‘Grantees Market’ highlighting the cheeses being made by our Cheesemaker grantees. It was not for sale as it was the end of the season for making this fresh Ewe’s milk cheese at the farm in Suffolk, but boy oh boy was it delicious. Now, it’s here, it’s in season and it’s wonderful!

This is an unusual cheese as it is a sheep milk log – not a goat log, but a sheep milk log and there are not many of those about. Sheeps’ milk is much sweeter and richer in flavour than goats’ and so if you are not keen on that slightly tart flavour of fresh goats’ milk you are in for a surprise with this cheese.

Made from the milk of local sheep that graze outside all year round, Pyghtle (old Suffolk word for small enclosure) is a lactic set cheese  – this means the slightly warm milk is left much longer to ferment and separate into curds and whey in its own time than non-lactic set cheeses (24-48 hours rather than a couple of hours in non-lactic set cheeses). This delicate curd is then ladled into moulds and after another day it is unmoulded, salted and left to mature for about a week.

items.title: Lucy’s April 2026 Cheese of the Month: Cuthman
items.excerpt: Meet Matt Gue, one-time vet turned farmer and now an award-winning cheese maker
items.body_html:
Every market there is a cheese that stops me in my tracks. ‘Cuthman’ (named after a local Saint from Steyning, where it is made) did exactly that at the March market.

Matt  Gue is a vet, Matt is a farmer and now Matt is a cheesemaker. Matt is also really part of the Cheesewick family as we have been lucky enough to share in his cheese making journey offering him one of our Chiswick Cheese Makers Grants in 2025. To see this cheese perfected to such an extraordinarily high standard gives me a very broad smile. Matt returned to the family farm after practicing as a vet for 6 years and after a chance meeting with Johnny Crickmore of Fen Farm Dairy (Baron Bigod) was inspired to use their own milk to make a cheese that would link their land, their herd and the irlocal community. Loving the pairing of Chaource cheese and Champagne Matt wanted to create a triple cream cheese that would pair beautifully with locally made sparkling wine, and I can say he has done that in spades. This cheese is a triumph!

This cheese is creamy, in both texture and taste, but more interestingly it is buttery, with grassy notes showing off the impeccable care with which the herd is reared and the pasture kept. For me, it has a subtle taste of honey at the end – there is no honey in this cheese, it’s simply the gorgeous sweetness that tricks my brain that there must be honey in there somewhere!. Congratulations Matt on winning a Silver Medal at the British and Irish Cheese Awards – what a feat in your first full year as a cheesemaker!

I did indeed enjoy it with a fizz – a Crémant de Bourgogne to be precise which had nutty overtones and paired with this delightful little cheese perfectly. It is fantastic with fresh apples or pears, or on any cheeseboard but I also dolloped it over some roast vegetables to make quite the midweek gourmet feast. This cheese is a stand-alone joy but pairs with many foods and with summer coming up is perfect with salads and pasta dishes.

Adur Valley Cuthman represents the best of British artisan cheesemaking, combining traditional techniques with a passion for quality and sustainability. It offers a unique taste experience that honours the land, the animals, and the people who make it. Cuthman cheese stands as a shining example of British Artisan dairy excellence – I love it and I’m sure you will too when you try it!

‘Cuthman’

Made by Matt Gue at Adur Valley East Sussex

Milk: raw cows’ milk

Age: 2-3 weeks

items.title: World Champion cheese maker Puis Hitz visits the Chiswick Cheese Market.
items.excerpt: World Champion cheese maker Puis Hitz visits the Chiswick Cheese Market. by Fran Warde What a triumphant day we had…
items.body_html:
World Champion cheese maker Puis Hitz visits the Chiswick Cheese Market.

by Fran Warde

What a triumphant day we had at the Chiswick Cheese Market! The sky was blue, shoppers arrived in their droves, and our stalls were filled with outstanding cheeses, including many winners from the British and Irish Cheese Awards.

The day was crowned by a very special visit from Puis Hitz, the 2025 World Champion cheesemaker of Le Gruyère AOP from the Vorderfuligen Swiss mountain dairy.

His cheese was selected as the best out of more than 5,500 cheeses from around the world, judged by 250 global experts who sniffed, tasted, and inspected each entry.

After progressing through multiple rounds, it reached the final lineup of 14 Supreme Champions, where Puis’s cheese was ultimately chosen. Our very own Perry Wakeman championed it for its rich, brothy umami flavour — a cheese that simply calls you back for more.

It was a great day for the Swiss!

We were honoured to welcome such a globally recognised cheesemaker to the market.

Puis spent time wandering the stalls, tasting cheeses, meeting makers and mongers, and appreciating everything the market has to offer.

Alfie from The European Fine Cheese Company, who imports Puis’s champion cheese, had it available on his stall and described meeting the maker as a “career high.”

Puis enjoyed chatting with Roger of White Lake Cheese about his wonderful award-winning goat’s cheeses. Justin of No. 2 Pound Street shared his Stichelton, which Puis greatly appreciated for its balance and rich paste.

Bianca Mora offered superb nuggets of Parmigiano Reggiano. When asked about his favourite British cheese, Puis paused thoughtfully before saying, “The British make great blue cheese.”

Puis runs a highly traditional, carefully regulated dairy set in green pastures just outside Bern. He produces eight wheels of cheese a day, seven days a week, using milk from six local farmers who all live within one kilometre of the dairy. The milk is delivered fresh each morning and evening.

This rich, pasture-fed milk is gently warmed in copper vats, and cultures are added to begin the transformation into cheese. The curds are then poured into moulds, pressed, and shaped before being taken down to the cellar and soaked in a brine bath for 24 hours. After this, the cheeses are placed on shelves, where they are brushed daily, washed with brine, and rubbed with a little dry salt for the first 10 days. Over the following 18 months, they are carefully turned and monitored until the final result emerges: the world champion Le Gruyère AOP Vorderfuligen all made under the skilled eye of Puis Hitz who joined us at the Chiswick Cheese Market on Sunday 19 April.

items.title: Gredos Goat’s Curd Basque Cheesecake
items.excerpt: This recipe comes from a dream collaboration of Brindisa and La Maritxu who both have stalls; Lucia and Monika are…
items.body_html:
This recipe comes from a dream collaboration of Brindisa and La Maritxu who both have stalls; Lucia and Monika are also big fans of the Chiswick Cheese Market.

The exceptional curd cheese that Brindisa import is a raw milk, from the Gredos mountains in Ávila where the goats roam the rich pastures grazing. It has an a ricotta like texture and adds a light goat’s milk flavour and citrusy notes to this delicious cheese cake.

Ingredients

270g Gredos Goats Curd, available Brindisa

330g Cream Cheese (any brand)

200g Caster sugar

1/4 tsp fine sea salt

4 large eggs (room temperature)

300g Double Cream (heavy cream)

Before you begin: take all the ingredients out of the fridge 1-2 hours before baking. Room temperature ingredients blend more smoothly and create a better texture.

Preheat your oven: Set to 220C fan or 240 conventional fan.

Prepare your tin: Line your 20cm springform tin with two overlapping sheets of parchment paper, pressing into the corners. The paper should come up above the sides of the tin by 5cm.

Method

Weigh out the sugar and salt in a small bowl and mix together. Set aside.

Combine the cheeses: Add the full tub of Gredos goat’s curd and cream cheese to the bowl of your stand mixer fitted with the padel attachment. Add the sugar and salt mixture.

Using a stand mixer: Beat on medium speed for 4-5 minutes until completely smooth and creamy, scraping down the sides of the bowl half way through.

Mixing by hand: If you don’t have a stand mixer use a large bowl and electric hand mixer, or a sturdy whisk. Beat vigorously for 6-8 minutes until the mixture is completley smooth and without lumps. Your arm will get a workout but it’s worth it!

Add the eggs one at a time: Crack in one egg and mix on a low speed (or stir by hand) until just incorporated before adding the next. Scrape down the sides between additions. Don’t overmix- you want to avoid incorporating too much air.

Pour in the double cream: Add the cream and mix on a low speed until just combined. If mixing by hand fold gently with a spatula or whisk slowly until smooth.

Check the consistency: The batter should be thick and pourable, like double cream – not watery or lumpy. If you see lumps gently whisk or strain through a sieve.

Pour into the prepared tin: Pour the better into your lined springform tin. Give it a gentle tap on the counter to release any air bubbles.

Bake for 30-35 minutes: The cheesecake is ready when the top is deeply golden brown (almost burnt looking) and the cake has risen but still has a pronounced wobble in the centre when you gently shake the tin.

Cool completely: Remove the cheesecake from the oven and leave it to rest at room temperature for 3-4 hours. The centre will sink and settle. Once cooled, refrigerate for at least 4 hours or overnight before serving.

Tips for sucess

Don’t be afraid of the colour: A true Basque cheesecake should have a dark, almost burnt top. The caramelisation adds incredible flavour.

The Wobble test: When done, the outer edge should be just set but the centre should still jiggle like a jelly. It will firm up as it cools.

If it browns too quickly: If the top is dark but the cake hasn’t risen. turn off the oven and leave the cake inside with the door closed for an extra 10-15 minutes.

Serving: Best served at room temperature or slightly chilled. Remove from the fridge 30 minutes before serving for the creamiest texture.

Storage: Keep refrigerated for up to 5 days. The flavour actually improves after a day or two!

items.title: Lucy’s March 2026 Cheese of the Month: Pi
items.excerpt: The Life of Pi – a beautiful Spanish sheep’s cheese
items.body_html:
The north part of Spain produces some excellent cow’s milk cheeses but as you travel further south and the land becomes drier, rockier and hotter the cheeses are virtually all sheep and goat milk. 50km south of Madrid and you come into Manchego country where cheeses must be made from the milk of local Manchega sheep to gain the name. We probably all know the sweet milky taste of a Manchego Fresco (young and fresh) and the bolder taste and granular chew of Manchego Curado or Viejo (mature and extra mature) but I was stopped in my tracks by Pi on Brindisa’s new stall at the Market. Made from the same milk, made in the same the area but this cheese is a world apart in both flavour and texture to its more familiar cousin.

Visually, it reminded me of a little artisan Caerphilly with its dark grey/blue rind and its clean white paste inside. Produced on the Hualda Farm near Toledo this is a raw sheep milk cheese with traditional rennet and is called ‘Pi’ (the Ancient Greek for the letter P). ‘P’ stands for the Penicillium Roqueforti added to the starter culture. This is the culture added to all blue cheeses and if pierced grows those familiar blue pathways inside cheese.

This cheese is not pierced, so the only hint of the growth of the mould is the dark inky blue colour speckled over the rind, but the influence on the flavour for me is dramatic. The silky creamy texture of the paste with its milky, lactic, buttery flavour, marrying with the mushroom hint of the rind was magic enough, but at the end of my mouthful there was an intense savoury flavour that I would expect from a cheese much older than its 4-6 weeks. And there we are – that is what that flavour is – it is a blue cheese, but don’t panic non-blue lovers – it is not a blue cheese! The Penicillium Roqueforti brings a roundness and boldness to what is quite a young sheep cheese. It’s pretty, it’s delicate and the flavour is robust – all at the same time.

Pi: it’s only blue on the outside

Make sure you get it out of the fridge at least 1 hour before eating as the flavours are completely different after time at room temperature. I enjoyed it with herby red Vermouth from Kevin at Vinagogo and it was excellent with a full-bodied Riesling. Food-wise it was fab with a charred baby gem but also married well with sun-blushed tomatoes and was gorgeous with sourdough. The firm and springy texture when young becomes almost spreadable with time. This cheese is ‘quietly very exciting’.

Brindisa imports all things Spanish, and their cheese range is huge, but they are specialising in sheep milk cheese for us. Sheep’s milk is the backbone of Spanish cheesemaking. Spain is home to many rare and traditional dairy breeds, each producing milk with its own character. Brindisa feels that by championing these cheeses, they will help preserve the knowledge, culture and biodiversity behind them. They want to really show them off and teach us about them. Visit their stall on Sunday and start your Spanish sheep cheese journey.

items.title: The 2025 World Cheese Awards, A Judge’s View by Fran Warde
items.excerpt: The 2025 World Cheese Awards Consume Bern, Switzerland
items.body_html:
Take 5,244 cheeses from more than 46 countries. Gather 265 expert judges in one vibrant city — in 2025, that city was Bern, Switzerland. Add the incredible Guild of Fine Food, the team behind the prestigious World Cheese Awards — and let the magic begin.

As dawn breaks on 13th November 2025 judges stream into the BernExpo’s Festhalle to be greeted by a breathtaking sight: more than 110 long tables laden with a cornucopia of cheeses. There are no labels, no clues to origin or maker, only discreet barcodes. Aprons are tied on — very yellow and smart ones at that — glasses of water are poured to keep palates clean, and the room hums with chatter as old friends reunite and first-time judges take it all in. The excitement is unmistakable.

Fran Warde, Perry Wakeman & New Zealand judge at the start of the day

When John Farrand, Managing Director of the Guild of Fine Food, calls the room to order, the energy sharpens into focus. He calmly briefs everyone on the process for the day. Many judges are seasoned veterans of the awards; for others, it is their first experience of judging on this scale. Soon they head to their designated tables, meet their fellow team, switch on their iPads, gather knives and cheese irons, and take a moment to decide where to begin.

Strategy is part instinct, part experience. Perhaps start with the younger, softer-looking cheeses and build towards the harder styles and powerful blues. Yet it is all educated guesswork. Some cheeses sit whole and proud, others are cut; some wear washed or vividly coloured rinds, others appear pale and understated. Appearances can be deceptive.

For the next three to four hours the hall settles into deep cheese concentration. Judges examine each of their 40 plus cheeses carefully, assessing appearance, inhaling aroma, feeling the body and texture, and finally tasting, analysing flavour and balance. Scores are entered into iPads and medals are awarded: Bronze, Silver and Gold. From the Gold medal winners, each table must agree on one exceptional cheese — their Super Gold — to send forward to the Super Jury.

In a change for 2025, the Super Jury, a panel of 14 internationally respected cheesemongers, makers and affineurs did not participate in the morning judging to ensure their palates remained fresh for the final decision. While anticipation builds for the afternoon finale, the other judges enjoy a well-earned lunch and the lively Capital of Cheese celebrations taking place across the venue. Tastings, bustling markets and masterclasses fill the space, alongside traditional Swiss horn playing and, from The Academy of Cheese, the exhilarating Young Cheesemaker of the Year competition. The young finalists display remarkable composure, presenting and performing in front of such an esteemed audience, they propose a cheeseboard, cutting and wrapping challenge, cheese identification, a perfect pairing with Peters Yard crackers and a MasterRind quiz. The winner was Hannah Lee a monger from Uplands Cheese in Wisconsin, USA.

items.title: Whipped Feta and Greens Summer Salad by Fran Warde
items.excerpt: This vibrant summer salad brings colour and flavour to your table, perfect as a centrepiece or an addition to a…
items.body_html:
This vibrant summer salad brings colour and flavour to your table, perfect as a centrepiece or an addition to a BBQ. The whipped feta adds a delightful touch to summer vegetables.

Serves: 4
Prep Time: 40 minutes
Ingredients:
200g Feta or other soft cheese
125g thick yoghurt
1 clove garlic
1 tsp Dijon mustard
½ lemon, zested and juiced
200g peas, shucked
200g sugar snap peas
200g runner beans
Small bunch flat-leaf parsley
Small bunch mint
3 tbsp olive oil
Freshly ground black pepper
Sprinkling of sea salt
Instructions:
Prepare the Whipped Feta:
In an electric blender, combine the feta, yoghurt, garlic, Dijon mustard, lemon zest, and lemon juice.
Blend until smooth and creamy.
Place in the fridge to chill and thicken.

Prepare the Vegetables:
If using fresh peas, shuck them.
Slice the sugar snap peas in half lengthways.
Slice the runner beans at an angle.
Blanch the peas, sugar snap peas, and runner beans in boiling water for 2 minutes for a crunchy texture or 3-4 minutes for a softer texture.
Drain the vegetables and refresh them in iced water until chilled to retain their bright green colour. Once chilled, drain well.

Assemble the Salad:
Spread the chilled whipped feta on a large serving plate, covering the entire surface.
Pick the leaves off the parsley and mint, and add them to the green vegetables. Toss to combine.
Arrange the vegetable and herb mixture on top of the whipped feta.

Garnish:
If you have nasturtiums in your garden, top the salad with a few flowers and smaller leaves for a pretty touch and a lightly peppery flavour.
Drizzle with olive oil and sprinkle with freshly ground black pepper and sea salt.

items.title: The Trethowan Brothers and the Jones brothers
items.excerpt: I was lucky enough to attend an unusual cheese event last week. The Trethowan Brothers (Pitchfork Cheddar) and the Jones…
items.body_html: I was lucky enough to attend an unusual cheese event last week. The Trethowan Brothers (Pitchfork Cheddar) and the Jones brothers (Lincolnshire Poacher cheese) have been running an experiment. One farm is in Somerset, one in Lincolnshire – different grass, different cows, different milk. The Trethowans went to Lincolnshire and the Jones’ went to Somerset and each made their own recipe cheeses using the milk and maturing rooms of the others’ dairy. Last week was the great ‘reveal’ of ‘Poachfork’. We gathered @thekernelbrewery to taste the different cheeses accompanied by some truly excellent beer! After being led through a tasting it was evident to everyone, the power of ‘affinage’. (Affinage – the art of maturing cheese). Where and how the cheeses had been stored over the year or so they were maturing had made such a vast difference to the texture, colour and taste of the cheeses. Although both were recognisable as themselves (the Pitchfork was still a Pitchfork and the Poacher very much still a Poacher) there was a marked difference in the Poacher made and stored in the Pitchfork dairy with its maturing rooms alive with the friendly bacteria of the Pitchfork cheddars and vice versa. Thank you @trethowanbrothers and @lincolnshirepoacher for a fabulous and educational evening.

items.excerpt: Which brings me onto to some home news – @cheese_academy are hosting ‘Affineur of the Year’ again next month. Only…
items.body_html:
Which brings me onto to some home news – @cheese_academy are hosting ‘Affineur of the Year’ again next month.

Only 4 years old, this event has quickly become both one of the most important and one of the most fun events in the cheese calendar. There are four categories – Cheddar, Blue, Washed Rind and Brie. Each candidate receives their very young cheeses from the same batch on the same day. The maturing times are different for each cheese. The makers – @quickescheese, @cropwellbishopcreamery, @whitelakecheese and @fenfarmdairy mature several of the cheeses from that batch in their own dairies to act as ‘controls’.

On the 3rd of June the artisan cheese world will gather, and the cheeses will be judged. There is a winner in each category and an overall ‘Affineur of the year’ is crowned. The Cheese Market sponsors the Cheddar category but this year the Cheese Market team has turned into an entrant! We received our Blue Shropshire at 2 weeks old on March 10th and she has been maturing in my Thameside cellar since. Sitting next door to the Bell and Crown on the Strand, separated from barrels of beer we decided that we would like to bring a little ‘chiswickness’ to her and she has been sitting next to a pint of London Pride for the duration of her maturation. We are also hoping that the yeast from the beer will help the flavour profile. To allow the blue mould to grow we ‘pierced’ her at 5 weeks and have been turning her, controlling the humidity and temperature and generally loving her every day since. A team rota was set up and daily trips to the river cellar are now the ‘norm’ in our lives. Our cheese ‘baby’ is growing up and we are hopeful we have created a fabulous ‘cheesewick’ blue! Watch this space for an update and we hope to have our cheese at the market in June for tasting!

items.title: Chicory, Pear, Hazelnut and Goat’s Cheese Salad
items.excerpt: When thinking about flavours for a salad, it is worth considering what the principal ingredient is traditionally served with. For example, cheese…
items.body_html:
When thinking about flavours for a salad, it is worth considering what the principal ingredient is traditionally served with. For example, cheese goes with pears, apples or grapes, all of which could supply the sweetness in this salad. The caramelized pears are delicious, but so, it must be said, are perfectly ripe raw ones, sliced at the last minute (or sliced in advance and kept from browning under water.

The other matters to consider are texture (it’s good to have some crunch, supplied here by the nuts) and colour (which is what the red chicory and watercress are partly for. Without them the whole dish would be white).

SERVES 4

15g/ 1/2oz butter

1 tsp light brown soft sugar

4 small ripe pears, peeled,

cored and quartered

1 red chicory

1 white chicory

a small handful of watercress

200g/7oz goat’s cheese log

20g/ 3/4oz/2 tbsp hazelnuts, toasted

and roughly chopped, to serve

For the dressing

1 tbsp red wine vinegar

3 tbsp extra-virgin olive oil

salt and black pepper

  1. Heat the grill (broiler) to high.
  2. Melt the butter and sugar in a frying pan on a medium heat until the sugar has dissolved. Add the pears and fry until lightly caramelized (about 3 minutes). Remove to a plate and cool.
  1. In a large bowl, whisk together the dressing ingredients.
  2. Cut the ends off both chicory and separate the leaves.

Add the chicory leaves and the watercress to the dressing in the bowl, and turn gently to coat the leaves.

  1. Cut the goat’s cheese into 4 equal slices (see hack).
  2. Place the cheese slices on an oven tray and grill

(broil) for 1 minute, or until the top of the cheese is golden and bubbling.

  1. On a large serving plate, or on four individual plates, arrange the salad, caramelized pears and grilled goat’s cheese. Sprinkle with the toasted hazelnuts, to serve.

Credit is: Life’s Too Short to Stuff a Mushroom by Prue Leith, £25 Carnival. Photography Ant Duncan

items.excerpt: Serves 4 FOR THE BRAISED LEEKS 130g salted butter 2 teaspoons vadouvan spice 200g shredded leeks FOR THE CARROT DIP…
items.body_html:
Serves 4

FOR THE BRAISED LEEKS
130g salted butter
2 teaspoons vadouvan spice
200g shredded leeks

FOR THE CARROT DIP
1 sweet potato
3 carrots, peeled and roughly
chopped
100g red lentils
salt and pepper

TO ASSEMBLE
4 thin sourdough bread slices
olive oil
140g Caerphilly cheese
(or a tangy territorial cheese,
see note)
pinch of garam masala

This dish uses one of my favourite cheeses – Caerphilly. I’m not talking about those bland plastic-wrapped Caerphillies that supermarkets sell. I’m talking about traditional Caerphilly with a velvet grey rind, crumbly centre, and delicious fudgy texture just beneath the rind. Vadouvan is a French-Indian spice blend. It has all the spices you’d expect from curry powder but also shallot and garlic. You can find it in Waitrose or online, or replace it with a mild curry powder.

To make the braised leeks

• Melt the butter in a pan over a low heat and add the vadouvan spice.
Once the butter is fragrant, add the leeks and cook over a low heat to braise for 45 minutes until the butter has lightly browned and the leeks are softly stewed. Allow to cool and put aside for later.

To make the carrot dip
• Preheat the oven to 200°C (400°F), Gas Mark 6.
• Wrap the sweet potato in aluminium foil and bake in the oven for 45–50 minutes until soft. Once cooked, unwrap and peel off the skin.

FOR THE BRAISED LEEKS

130g salted butter

2 teaspoons vadouvan spice

200g shredded leeks

FOR THE CARROT DIP

1 sweet potato

3 carrots, peeled and roughly

chopped

100g red lentils

salt and pepper

4 thin sourdough bread slices

olive oil

140g Caerphilly cheese

(or a tangy territorial cheese,

see note)

pinch of garam masala

This dish uses one of my favourite cheeses – Caerphilly. I’m not talking about those bland plastic-wrapped Caerphillies that supermarkets sell. I’m talking about traditional Caerphilly with a velvet grey rind, crumbly centre, and delicious fudgy texture just beneath the rind. Vadouvan is a French-Indian spice blend. It has all the spices you’d expect from curry powder but also shallot and garlic. You can find it in Waitrose or online, or replace it with a mild curry powder.

 

To make the braised leeks

• Melt the butter in a pan over a low heat and add the vadouvan spice.

items.title: Why Spring Cheeses Are Special
items.excerpt: Spring feels as if it has sprung with hints of warmth in the sun and as regulars you probably already know that means the fresh young spring cheeses will start to appear at the market.
items.body_html:
Spring feels as if it has sprung with hints of warmth in the sun and as regulars you probably already know that means the fresh young spring cheeses will start to appear at the market. Why are they special? – well, the animals are eating the fresh spring grass and shoots in the fields and the milk becomes sweeter. A few of my favourites to look out for:

Mothais (@thefrenchcomte) – a young French goat’s cheese wrapped in a chestnut leaf. The leaf first takes the moisture from the cheese then allows the cheese to keep moisture as it ripens adding a few hints of undergrowth and forest floor to the flavours. This is a great cheese at other times of the year but in spring it becomes very special.

Robiola Capra (@gastronomicamarket) Medhi brings us several versions of Robiola made with goat, sheep or cow milk or a mix of all three. My personal recommendation is the Capra (goat) as it has a wonderful acidity when fresh and firm at about 2 weeks old but ripens into a gooey unctuous strong flavoured cheese.


Images: Le Mothais, Robiola 3 Latti, Lucky Marcel

Lucky Marcel is making its first appearance at our market. This is a new cheese from @felthamsfarm and is basking in the glory of winning a super-gold award at the World Cheese Awards in November.
This is even more special at this time of the year when the fresh lush grass is appearing, so taste this on @no2poundst and I’m sure you’ll be a convert. Lovely citrus flavours at about a fortnight old when it is firm, but it takes on much bolder flavours and a gooey texture as it ripens.

items.title: What’s On: March is for melting Cheese
items.excerpt: We’ll have pots of hot cheese to try from 9.30am. Roberto and Joel will bring along bags of their ready mixed cheeses for fondue to sell so you can replicate the full flavours at home.
items.body_html:
March is for melting Cheese

Were the last few days just a hint of spring to come and winter is still with us perhaps? With the ski season in full swing we still have thoughts of snow and fondues so we have dedicated this March market to melting cheese.

Free tasting on HQ of @thefrenchcomte secret fondue blend. We’ll have pots of hot cheese to try from 9.30am. Roberto and Joel will bring along bags of their ready mixed cheeses for fondue to sell so you can replicate the full flavours at home.

@theroebuckchiswick will be serving their raclette as usual using traditional farmhouse French raclette cheese. If you want to make it at home @thefrenchcomte will be bringing plenty of varieties of raclette – truffle, peppercorn, mature and raw milk so you can mix and match at home with your own machines.

What about melting some British cheeses I hear you say? As a real treat Fay @bigwheelcheese is bringing her tartiflette griddle and you will be able to try this Mountain French delight made with Raedbald – a new British Reblochon style cheese made in East Anglia by @fenfarmdairy (of Baron Bigod fame). Wow! I can’t wait for that!

A French/British battle of the melts? Try them and see what you think.

Images: Tartiflette from Big Wheel Cheese, Raedwald from Fen Farm Dairy, Raclette from The Roebuck

Grate & Grill and Amuse Bouche will be serving their galettes and toasties with plenty of melted cheese respectively. Bring on that melty, gooey, oozey gorgeous hot cheese!

Special Guest: Michele of Napoli on the Road

At noon we have a very special treat because Michele founder of Napoli on the Road is joining Steve on his book stall next door to HQ. Michele was voted the best pizza chef on the planet in 2023 and Napoli on The Road won best pizza restaurant in Europe in 2024.

He will bring along copies of his wonderful new recipe book to sign and he says there may well be some pizza to try – ‘The Cheesewick’ pizza at his restaurant is named after our market!

Note to self – come hungry to taste ALL the melted cheeses.

items.title: What’s new this Month – Punch Drunk Love!
items.excerpt: February is the month of love, A day out at Chiswick Cheese Market and he can choose all the cheese we buy!
items.body_html:
February is the month of love and my other half is getting a card from me with a handmade gift token in it – ‘A day out at Chiswick Cheese Market and he can choose all the cheese we buy!’ – Well, if that in itself is not a gift worth giving to any cheese lover then can we tempt you further as we have something very special lined up for this ‘Valentine’ Market. Max from Drunk cheese will be hosting a free tasting session on HQ.

When I first met Max, I thought that ‘drunk cheese’ sounded gimmicky but I discovered that was far from the truth. Its history goes back to the 1st World War when the farmers in Northern Italy hid their cheese in empty wine barrels from the looting Austro-Hungarian troops. The pomace (grape skins) left in the barrels macerated the ageing cheese and ‘Ubriaco’ or drunk cheese was born.

These days it is an art in itself, and is much broader than using just wine residue – a Super-Gold was won at this year’s World Cheese Awards for their ‘Blugins’ cheese which is coated in juniper berries and steeped in gin (and if you are both a blue cheese and gin lover I do encourage you to try this one!).So, both those already converted and those new to ‘drunk cheese’ join us on HQ for a fascinating tasting starting at 9.30am.
